subject: ventures/ppp-pricing-table-generator
professional: a SaaS pricing manager who sets regional (PPP) price lists in Paddle, Stripe or an app store; first checks: are the price levels sourced and current, do the floor and cap actually hold after rounding, and is the break-even arithmetic right

evidence.correctness: The arithmetic matches an independent Python model (scratchpad ppp/indep.py, written from the README's method: (index/100)^strength, clamp to floor/cap, nearest .99): default base 29 gives US 28.99, DE 26.99 (factor 0.9144), PL 16.99, BR 15.99 (0.5357), NG 11.99, IN 10.99 (0.3789), identical to `node -e buildTable({base:29})`; revenue what-if for EXAMPLE_SHARES at 2% / elasticity 1.5 is 580.00 -> 703.95 (+21.37%) in both; breakEvenLift(0.4)=0.6667 = 1/(1-d)-1, and the guide's table (20% +25%, 40% +67%, 70% +233%) checks by hand. Two output faults: (1) at the defaults the floor is broken by rounding: PK clamps to 0.35*29 = 10.15 and charm-rounds down to 9.99 (34.4% of base, 65% off); (2) 'nine' rounding at base 25 prices the US (reference market, cap 1) at 29, a 16% premium, and tiers with cap 1.2 charge the US 32.99 on a 29 base. The data the method runs on was checked against World Bank WDI (api.worldbank.org, PA.NUS.PRVT.PP / PA.NUS.FCRF, private-consumption price level, US=100; euro members via EMU FX), script ppp/compare.py: median absolute gap 4.3 index points for 2024 (3.9 for 2023), but Egypt 25 vs 15.3 (+63%), Thailand 41 vs 30.9 (+33%), China 60 vs 49.3, Norway 105 vs 88.8, Germany 88 vs 75.9, Peru 38 vs 51.9 (-27%), Mexico 47 vs 59.0, Brazil 41 vs 46.8. Reading-level fine, but several markets are off by a full discount group or more.
evidence.completeness: Ran `node --test '*.test.mjs'` and bare `node --test` (README): 30/30 pass. Checked each README/page feature: base-to-table for 49 countries (README 'about 50' holds), strength, floor, cap, four roundings, tiers 0-12 (tiers 12 -> 12 prices; tiers 4 -> 28.99/20.99/16.99/12.99), regional discount groups at nearest 5% (`node cli.mjs 29`), index overrides (parseIndexOverrides, US 50 -> IN 17.99), traffic-share revenue what-if (`node cli.mjs 29 --traffic shares.txt`), CSV and JSON export (`--format csv|json`), guide page, opt-out local usage counts. Served page https://marisstella.app/ppp-pricing-table-generator/ returns 200 and its ppp.mjs is byte-identical to the source. No stubs or TODOs. Every claimed feature works end to end.
evidence.verification: 30 tests pass. They pin roundPrice cases, the floor with rounding 'none', the US at 28.99, tier count, overrides, break-even lift and the revenue model's sign at elasticity 0.5/1/2. Six mutants seeded with quality_mutate.py: 3 caught (floor clamp removed, top tier price changed, 'nine' rounding shifted), 3 survived (conversion cap Math.min(1, ...) removed at ppp.mjs:154; discount groups rounded to 10% instead of 5% at ppp.mjs:167; refIndex replaced by 100 at ppp.mjs:52, which only differs when the US index is overridden). No test runs the floor or cap together with charm/nine rounding, which is how the default-settings floor breach got through (ppp.test.mjs:59 uses rounding 'none').
evidence.craft: Read ppp.mjs (204 lines), cli.mjs (40), index.html script (lines 137-216), usage.mjs, the three test files. Pure exported functions, validation shared by page and CLI, HTML escaped in table cells, usage storage guarded. Defects: rounding is applied after the floor/cap clamp with no re-check (ppp.mjs:109); CLI silently prints text for an unknown --format (cli.mjs:29: `--format xml` gives the text table) and ignores unknown flags; refCode is a buildTable parameter neither the page nor CLI can set; the top tier's 'full price' comment (ppp.mjs:101) is wrong once cap > 1. Small, readable, a reviewer would accept it with those fixes.
evidence.claims: Backed: disclaimer 'No warranty ... not financial, tax or legal advice' on index.html:130 and the guide; 'never uploaded / no network calls' (grep finds no fetch/XHR/sendBeacon; page.test.mjs:166 asserts it; usage.mjs honours DNT/GPC at :34); 'about 50 countries' (49); indexes labelled 'rounded estimates' on page, README and CLI output; revenue model labelled a what-if; served copy has no placeholder origin (served-copy.mjs). Not backed: the floor is presented as a guarantee ('never go below this fraction', ppp.mjs:26; guide: 'The floor keeps any price above a share of your base') but rounding undercuts it at the defaults (PK 9.99 < 10.15); the cap is labelled '1 = never above base' (index.html:56) but 'nine' rounding and tiers with cap > 1 put the reference market above base. 'In the spirit of the World Bank ICP price levels' is roughly fair (median gap ~4 points) but gives no year or source table, and several values are off by 25-60%.
evidence.fitness: Walked an indie developer's job: enter 29, strength 0.7, floor 0.35, read the table and the 13 discount groups, paste a traffic mix and see +21.4% at elasticity 1.5, copy CSV. It produces a usable starting price list in a minute and the break-even column is a real aid. A practitioner still has to re-source the price levels (several markets off a full group), convert to local currency and price endings in the processor, and check the floor by eye.
evidence.domain: Against common PPP-pricing practice (price-level ratio from ICP/World Bank PPP over market FX, damped with an exponent or blend, floor, a small number of tiers, prices set by billing country) the method is the standard one and the break-even rule 1/(1-d)-1 is correct. Departs where a pricing manager would object: the price levels are undated and uncited (Egypt still at 25 after the 2024 devaluation, WDI 15.3; Peru 38 vs 51.9), rounding is not constrained by the floor/cap the user set, the top tier charges every member the maximum (GB, factor 0.855, pays the full 28.99 with tiers 4), and the constant-elasticity what-if uses one elasticity for all markets (disclosed).

mutations.change: return clamp(raw, o.floor, o.cap); -> return clamp(raw, 0, o.cap);
a = v * Math.min(1, newConv) * r.price -> a = v * newConv * r.price
const f = top ? hi : members -> const f = top ? hi * 0.9 : members

defects.what: Rounding is applied after the floor/cap clamp and never re-checked, so the user's floor and cap do not hold: at the defaults (base 29, floor 0.35, charm) Pakistan is 9.99 (34.4% of base, below 10.15); 'nine' rounding at base 25 prices the US at 29 with cap 1 (a 16% premium on the reference market, shown as a -16% discount). The floor and cap are presented as guarantees on the page, in DEFAULTS and in the guide.

Built-in price levels are undated and uncited ('in the spirit of' ICP). Against World Bank WDI 2024 private-consumption price levels: Egypt 25 vs 15.3, Thailand 41 vs 30.9, China 60 vs 49.3, Norway 105 vs 88.8, Germany 88 vs 75.9, Peru 38 vs 51.9, Mexico 47 vs 59.0; several markets land a full 5% discount group or more off.

With tiers and cap > 1, the top band is priced at the highest factor for every member, so the reference market pays above base (cap 1.2, tiers 4: US 32.99 on a 29 base), contradicting the comment that the top band 'keeps the full price'; with cap 1 every top-band member (GB, factor 0.855) pays the full base.

3 of 6 seeded core mutants survive (conversion cap removed, discount groups at 10% instead of 5%, reference index hard-coded to 100). The floor test uses rounding 'none', so the default-settings floor breach is untested; no test pins a discount group's percentage or a non-US reference.
CLI silently falls back to the text table for an unknown --format (e.g. xml) and ignores unknown flags.

verdict: A small, honest, working PPP price-table generator whose arithmetic is right: an independent Python model reproduces the default table (US 28.99, DE 26.99, BR 15.99, IN 10.99), the revenue what-if (580.00 -> 703.95, +21.37%) and the break-even rule 1/(1-d)-1 exactly, and every README feature runs from the page and the CLI; the served engine is byte-identical to the source and the no-network claim holds. A SaaS pricing manager would stop at two things. The floor and cap are not enforced after rounding, so the default settings price Pakistan at 9.99 under a 10.15 floor and 'nine' rounding can charge the US above base. And the built-in price levels, compared with World Bank 2024 private-consumption price levels, are close on median (4.3 points) but undated and off by 25-60% for Egypt, Thailand, Peru and Mexico. 30 tests pass, but 3 of 6 seeded mutants survive. Does not meet the bar: correctness 2, claims 2, verification 2, median 2. Finished (completeness 3). Fixable in one session: re-check floor/cap after rounding, refresh and date the index table from WDI, fix the top tier under cap > 1, and test the floor with charm rounding.
